 Responsibility for the protection of human subjects of research at the institutions of the UMaine System is largely vested in the individual institutional IRB. In the United States, concern over the rights and welfare of humans involved in research prompted changes in grant policy. In 1974 Congress enacted the National Research Act (P.L. 93-348) establishing a National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. In 1979, the National Commission published the now well-known Belmont Report that identified three basic ethical principles as relates to human subjects research. The principles are; respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. In January 1981, human subjects regulations were amended to provide a common framework within which Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) could review human subjects research. The regulations were codified in 1991 under Title 45, Part 46 of the Code of Federal Regulations. Subpart A of the codification was accepted by seventeen Federal Agencies as “the Common Rule.”

claude-search.title: Ethical LLM-Assisted Research: A Framework for Responsible Delegation, Verification, and Epistemic Value
claude-search.snippet:
#### 4.3 Failure of Accountable Delegation

Consider a technically convincing LLM-generated section whose citations, calculations, or central inferences have not been examined by the researcher. The required human-controlled verification cycle remains incomplete, V(g) = 0. Consequently, the claims cannot responsibly be presented as scientifically warranted.

The generation of unverified candidate material is a legitimate part of scientific exploration. The ethical failure occurs when such material enters a submitted scientific argument as warranted without adequate verification and authorial assessment. This effectively transfers part of the authors' checking obligations to reviewers, whose role is independent scrutiny rather than substitution for author verification.

A similar failure arises when a researcher accepts a complex AI-generated inference without sufficiently examining its supporting steps. Where an epistemic record exposes an unresolved inferential gap, responsible presentation requires further examination. Questions concerning possible unacknowledged intellectual contributions may additionally require investigation of information provenance.

These failures concern the exercise of human guidance control and responsibility rather than the machine origin of the material. The same principles apply to fully human research when authors present claims whose evidential or inferential support they have not adequately examined.

#### § 21.123 Early termination of research support: Evaluation of applications and proposals.

(a) The department or agency head may require that Federal department or agency support for any project be terminated or suspended in the manner prescribed in applicable program requirements, when the department or agency head finds an institution has materially failed to comply with the terms of this policy.

(b) In making decisions about supporting or approving applications or proposals covered by this policy the department or agency head may take into account, in addition to all other eligibility requirements and program criteria, factors such as whether the applicant has been subject to a termination or suspension under paragraph (a) of this section and whether the applicant or the person or persons who would direct or has/have directed the scientific and technical aspects of an activity has/have, in the judgment of the department or agency head, materially failed to discharge responsibility for the protection of the rights and welfare of human subjects (whether or not the research was subject to federal regulation).
